name: Methodist Split of 1844
summary: The division of the Methodist Episcopal Church, then the largest American denomination, into Northern and Southern churches after its General Conference asked a slaveholding bishop to stop serving.

start.label: General Conference asks Bishop James O. Andrew, a slaveholder, to stop serving as bishop

end.label: Methodist Episcopal Church, South, organized at Louisville

background.text: Wesley and early American Methodists condemned slavery, but the church relaxed its rules to grow in the South; abolitionists who pressed the issue, such as Orange Scott, were disciplined and in 1843 left to form the Wesleyan Methodist Connection.

happened.text: Bishop James O. Andrew of Georgia had become a slaveholder through inheritance and marriage. The 1844 General Conference voted 111 to 69 that he 'desist from the exercise of this office so long as this impediment remains'.
Southern delegates protested, and the conference adopted a Plan of Separation allowing the Southern conferences to form their own church.
The Methodist Episcopal Church, South, was organized at Louisville in May 1845.

participants.name: James O. Andrew
participants.role: Slaveholding bishop at the center of the dispute

participants.name: Orange Scott
participants.role: Abolitionist who founded the Wesleyan Methodist Connection (1843)

outcomes.text: The Northern church repudiated the Plan of Separation in 1848, leading to a dispute over church property that the U.S. Supreme Court settled in the Southern church's favor in Smith v. Swormstedt (1854).
The split foreshadowed the Civil War. The churches reunited only in 1939, with Black Methodists placed in a separate, segregated Central Jurisdiction until 1968.

condemnations.by: General Conference of the Methodist Episcopal Church
condemnations.reason: Bishop James O. Andrew asked to desist from serving as bishop while he held slaves
condemnations.status: Superseded when he joined the Southern church

persecution_note: No one was persecuted in the split itself; the issue was the enslavement of Black Americans, which Southern Methodists defended.

sources.citation: Donald G. Mathews, Slavery and Methodism: A Chapter in American Morality, 1780–1845. Princeton: Princeton University Press, 1965.
Russell E. Richey, Kenneth E. Rowe, and Jean Miller Schmidt, The Methodist Experience in America: A History. Nashville: Abingdon Press, 2010.
